papers.title_in_file: Quantum Machine Learning for Anomaly Detection in Consumer Electronics
papers.version_note: arXiv:2409.00294v1 [quant-ph] 30 Aug 2024. The text layer holds one copy of the paper and has 7 pages. Page numbers in the anchors count text-layer pages (form feeds), so they can differ from the page numbers of the stored anchors.
papers.what_it_is: A short survey that introduces a general QML workflow for anomaly detection, reviews variational, kernel, clustering, ensemble and reinforcement-learning QML methods, and summarizes five published case studies; it reports no experiment of its own.

existing.note: The sentence is in the discussion of reference [19] (Kyriienko and Magnusson). Table I lists the best average precision for that study; the paper gives no baseline figure in the text.
existing.value: The authors report, citing Kyriienko and Magnusson, that the quantum kernel-based classifier outperforms the classical kernel by 15% in average precision in an increased feature space.
quotes: the quantum kernel-based classifier outperforms the classical kernel by 15% in average precision in an increased feature space
existing.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work and does not test.
existing.reader_inference: The paper says nothing about which classical kernel, dataset size or number of qubits gave the 15%; the comparison is the cited study's, not this survey's.

existing.note: The paper ties the conclusion to the cost of the Gram matrix and of inference, which it states just before.
existing.value: The authors report, citing the same study, that the authors of that study concluded quantum kernel-based methods can be applied only for re-checking transactions and evaluating top-priority cases instead of mass evaluations in real time.
quotes: This time complexity led them to conclude that quantum kernel-based methods can be applied for only re-checking transactions and evaluating top-priority cases instead of mass evaluations in real time.
existing.certainty_reason: A conclusion the paper attributes to other work and does not test.

existing.value: The authors state that fitting raw data directly into the quantum circuit is challenging because of the limit on the number of usable qubits, so raw data is usually dimensionally reduced first.
quotes: Fitting raw data directly into the quantum circuit is challenging due to the limitation of the total number of usable qubits.
Therefore, in most cases, raw data is dimensionally reduced before fitting into a quantum circuit.
existing.certainty_reason: A statement about the field and its devices, not about the paper's own work.

existing.value: The authors state that the paper introduces QML and its applications for anomaly detection in consumer electronics, and includes five case studies of recent works.
quotes: In this work, we have introduced QML and its applications for anomaly detection in consumer electronics.
included five case studies of recent works to show their applications in anomaly detection in the consumer electronics field.
existing.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of its scope in the Abstract.

assertions.value: The authors state that they selected five case studies, on the Internet of Medical Things, surveillance, image processing, sensor intrusion and credit card fraud detection, to illustrate QML for anomaly detection in consumer electronics.
assertions.anchor: Section I, contributions list, text-layer p.1
quotes: we have selected five case studies on the Internet of Medical Things (IoMT), surveillance, image processing, sensor intrusion, and credit card fraud detection
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of the case-study scope (Section I).

assertions.value: The authors state that, to their knowledge, no comprehensive survey of anomaly detection by QML for consumer electronic devices exists, although surveys of anomaly detection with QML algorithms in general exist.
quotes: Though literature surveys on anomaly detection using QML algorithms exist [2], there is no such comprehensive survey considering the anomalies in consumer electronic devices, to our knowledge.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim about the literature, not checked in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors claim that classical machine learning models are insufficient to prevent all threats in a world where new types of anomalies emerge often, and that QML is emerging as a powerful computational tool that can detect anomalies more efficiently.
quotes: classical machine learning models are insufficient to prevent all the threats
Quantum Machine Learning (QML) is emerging as a powerful computational tool that can detect anomalies more efficiently.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim; the paper gives no measured comparison in support of it.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper runs no experiment of its own; the efficiency claim rests on the cited case studies, whose results are mixed and mostly simulated.

assertions.value: The authors state that classical ML algorithms used for anomaly detection systems, such as clustering, one-class SVMs, decision trees and neural networks, are very resource-intensive, take a long time to train, and suffer from over-fitting.
quotes: these algorithms are very resource-intensive and take a long time to train
They also suffer from over-fitting problems and find it challenging to adapt to new anomalies
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim about classical methods with no citation or measurement at that point.
assertions.reader_inference: No citation or data is given at the point of the claim.

assertions.value: The authors state that quantum machine learning has been deployed for consumer electronics applications such as credit card fraud detection, anomaly detection in surveillance, health care anomaly detection and crime prevention.
quotes: Quantum machine learning has been deployed for consumer electronics applications such as credit card fraud detection, anomaly detection in surveillance, health care anomaly detection, and crime prevention.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim about the field.
assertions.reader_inference: The case studies in the paper ran on simulators or on a cloud device for research, so 'deployed' is a loose word for what the paper shows.

assertions.value: The authors present a general framework of three steps for QML anomaly detection on classical data: clean the data and reduce its dimension, feed it to the QML circuit after quantum encoding and optimize the model on a classical computer, then feed new data to the trained model to predict whether it is an anomaly.
assertions.anchor: Fig. 1 caption and Section II-A, text-layer p.2
quotes: There are three significant steps to building a QML-based anomaly detection system.
The 1st step is to clean up the classical data and reduce the dimension as required.
In the 2nd step, we feed clean data into the QML circuit after quantum encoding and optimize the model with a classical computer.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own definition of its general framework (Fig. 1 caption).

assertions.value: The authors state that dimensionality reduction (for example LDA, PCA or t-SNE) is essential because existing quantum machines can handle only data of smaller dimension, owing to the limited number of qubits.
quotes: Dimensionality reduction is essential as the existing quantum machines can handle smaller dimensional data due to the limited number of qubits.
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement about the field and its devices.

assertions.value: The authors report that, in the case studies, they saw a trend of subsampling the original dataset before applying a quantum circuit, because quantum circuits cannot handle large volumes of data.
quotes: The quantum circuits can not handle large volumes
of data, so we saw a trend of subsampling the original dataset before application.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's observation across cited studies; the sentence is split by a page break in the text layer.
assertions.reader_inference: Section III gives one example: the hybrid autoencoder study trained on one week of observations.

assertions.value: The authors state that most researchers have used a hybrid approach, which yielded better results than the pure quantum approach.
quotes: Most researchers have used a hybrid approach, yielding better results than the pure quantum approach.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's summary of the cited studies; no comparison of hybrid against pure quantum models is shown in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that the case studies show the relevance of quantum machine learning in complex anomaly detection tasks that are currently solved by classical methods at the industrial scale.
quotes: The case studies show the relevance of quantum machine learning in complex anomaly detection tasks, which are currently solved by classical methods at the industrial scale.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's conclusion from cited studies.
assertions.reader_inference: Relevance is not the same as an advantage; the paper shows no case where a quantum model ran at industrial scale.

assertions.value: The authors state that the complex numbers alpha and beta in a superposition state represent the probability of the qubit collapsing to the state zero or the state one upon measurement.
quotes: α and β are complex numbers, representing the probability of the qubit collapsing to either |0⟩ or |1⟩ upon measurement.
assertions.certainty_reason: A textbook statement given loosely; the paper cites Nielsen and Chuang for the background.
assertions.reader_inference: Loose wording: alpha and beta are amplitudes, and the squared magnitudes are the probabilities.

assertions.value: The authors state that, if two qubits are entangled, measuring one qubit reveals the state of the other, and that these properties give quantum computers an edge over classical computers.
quotes: if two qubits are entangled, measuring one qubit reveals the state of the other
These properties give quantum computers an edge over classical computers.
assertions.certainty_reason: A general statement about quantum computing without proof or citation at that point.
assertions.reader_inference: The edge is asserted for quantum computers in general; the paper does not tie it to any anomaly detection result.

assertions.value: The authors state that, among many existing encoding techniques, angle encoding is the most popular for its simplicity, and that the paper restricts itself to classical anomaly detection problems.
quotes: Among many existing encoding techniques, angle encoding is the most popular for its simplicity
(We restrict it to only classical anomaly detection problems)
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement about the field; no survey of encodings is given.

assertions.value: The authors state that the ideal design of a variational quantum model is still an open question, and that expressivity is a good metric, referring to the sampling power of the circuit from a high-dimensional Hilbert space.
quotes: The ideal design of a variational quantum model is still an open question.
Expressivity is a good metric, referring to the sampling power of the circuit from a highdimensional Hilbert Space.
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement about the state of the field.

assertions.value: The authors describe a binary decision rule for a variational circuit: measure the first two qubits, add the expectation values for even and odd parity, and, for example, call the data an anomaly if the result has odd parity and normal otherwise.
quotes: We can make a binary decision after adding the expectation values for even and odd parity [7].
For example, if the result has odd parity, the data is an anomaly; otherwise, it is normal.
assertions.certainty_reason: A method described by example and attributed to reference [7]; not tested in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The odd-parity rule is an illustration, not a result; no parity rule is tied to a case-study result.

assertions.value: The authors describe a simple optimization strategy for a variational circuit, attributed to a cited reference: shift a parameter up by a small amount s and measure, shift it down by s and measure again, and subtract the results; they write the gradient as the difference of the two measured expectation values.
quotes: A simple optimization strategy can be calculating the gradient for any parameter by shifting the parameter by a small amount s and measuring the output
assertions.certainty_reason: A method attributed to reference [6] and stated without derivation or conditions.
assertions.reader_inference: The printed equation has no factor of one half and no condition on s; as printed, it is a finite difference that matches the exact shift rule only for specific gates and shift values.

assertions.value: The authors report that, in reference [8], the authors showed many near-term and fault-tolerant quantum models that can be realized through a general support vector machine can be replaced with a kernel that calculates the distance between encoded quantum states.
quotes: In [8], the authors showed that we can replace many near-term and faulttolerant quantum models that can be realized through a general support vector machine with a kernel that calculates the distance between encoded quantum states.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work (Schuld) and gives without conditions.

assertions.value: The authors state that a quantum kernel can map the data into a higher dimensional space where the anomalies will be linearly distinguishable from the standard data.
quotes: We can map the data into a higher dimensional space using a quantum kernel, where the anomalies will be linearly distinguishable from the standard data.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim stated without condition, proof or measurement.
assertions.reader_inference: Stated as a certainty ('will be'); separability depends on the kernel and the data, and the paper gives no condition.

assertions.value: The authors state that a hybrid quantum-classical neural network, shown in part (c) of Figure 2, performs more stably than a stand-alone PQC.
quotes: This integration is shown in part (c) of Figure 2, which performs more stably than a stand-alone PQC.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim without evidence at that point; the sentence points to reference [9] for more detail.

assertions.value: The authors report that, according to Rebentrost et al., quantum computers can evaluate inner products faster, meaning a faster evaluation of the kernel matrix, which enhances the speed of kernel methods such as QSVM.
quotes: According to Rebentrost et al. [10], quantum
computers can evaluate the inner products faster, meaning
faster evaluation of the kernel matrix. This property enhances
assertions.certainty_reason: A result attributed to other work; the paper gives no speed-up size or conditions.
assertions.reader_inference: No complexity, input-access assumption or data-loading cost is stated, and those conditions decide whether any speed-up holds.

assertions.value: The authors state that Rebentrost et al. proved that the training vectors can be represented as a superposition of basis states, and that the kernel can then be calculated by taking the partial trace of the corresponding density matrix, given as an equation.
quotes: The authors proved that given a 2n basis vector space |χ⟩, the
training vectors v⃗p can be represented as a superposition of the
by taking the partial trace of the corresponding density matrix
assertions.certainty_reason: A theorem the paper attributes to other work; the statement is not given with its conditions and the equation is garbled in the text layer.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer prints the dimension 2 to the power n as '2n'. Equation 1 is split over many lines by the layer and was not quoted.

assertions.value: The authors state that, in many problems, anomalies are highly similar to regular data, because an attacker will try not to get caught, and that in such cases a QSVM model that maps data in a high-dimensional vector space can distinguish anomalies from regular data.
quotes: In many problems, anomalies exhibit high similarity with regular data.
In such cases, a QSVM model that can access a high-dimensional vector space to map data can distinguish between anomalies and regular data.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim without evidence or conditions.
assertions.reader_inference: A classical kernel SVM also maps data to a high-dimensional space; the sentence does not say what the quantum model adds.

assertions.value: The authors report that Lloyd et al. proposed a method to calculate the distance between two real n-dimensional vectors with a swap test, which can find the nearest centroid for a feature vector, the main theme of clustering.
quotes: In [11], Lloyd et al. proposed a method to calculate the distance between two real, ndimensional vectors ⃗a and ⃗b with the help of a swap-test.
we can calculate the nearest centroid, which is the main theme of clustering.
assertions.certainty_reason: A method attributed to other work; the state preparation and cost are not given with their conditions.

assertions.value: The authors state that, using quantum clustering techniques, higher dimensional clustering makes it potentially possible to differentiate anomalies, since outliers usually refer to the anomalies.
quotes: In such cases, the outliers usually refer to the anomalies.
Using quantumclustering techniques, higher dimensional clustering makes it possible to differentiate anomalies potentially.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim with a hedge ('potentially') and no evidence.

assertions.value: The authors report that Antonio et al. proposed a quantum algorithm for an ensemble approach using bagging, and the authors state that its benefit comes from superposition, as a superposition of multiple transformations of the training data can be processed in parallel.
quotes: In [12], Antonio et al., proposed a quantum algorithm to implement an ensemble approach using bagging.
The benefit of the quantum ensemble algorithm comes from superposition, as we can generate a superposition of multiple transformations of training data and process them parallelly.
assertions.certainty_reason: A method attributed to other work, with a benefit claimed and not measured here.
assertions.reader_inference: The reference [12] lists A. Macaluso as the first author; the paper's text calls the author 'Antonio'.

assertions.value: The authors state that, because anomalous data is rare and a skewed dataset brings overfitting and bias, the majority vote from multiple learners in the quantum ensemble method means these problems can mostly be avoided.
quotes: In a skewed dataset comes the problem of overfitting and bias.
these problems can be mostly avoided.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim without evidence or conditions.
assertions.reader_inference: The argument holds for any majority-vote ensemble, classical or quantum; the paper gives no quantum-specific evidence.

assertions.value: The authors report that Dong et al. proposed a quantum reinforcement learning method with a value-updating framework inspired by superposition and parallelism, in which the action collapses to one of the eigen actions upon measurement and probability-amplitude updating is based on the Grover iteration.
quotes: In [13], Dong et al. proposed a novel QRL method.
It uses the collapse postulate, i.e., the action will collapse to one of the eigen actions upon measurement, to make its action-selection policy.
which occurs based on the Grover iteration [14].
assertions.certainty_reason: A method attributed to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that QRL can be used to build reliable anomaly detection systems, as a QRL-based system can constantly learn from new experiences with a reward and penalty system.
quotes: QRL can be used to build reliable ADS [15], as a QRLbased ADS can constantly learn from new experiences with a reward and penalty system.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim attributed to reference [15]; no measurement is given.

assertions.value: The authors report that, in the study of Rajawat et al. on security assessment of Internet of Medical Things devices, the quantum deep learning-based models achieved an accuracy ranging from 92.23% to 99.34%, compared against classical reinforcement learning agents, DNN, CNN and quantum DNN.
assertions.anchor: Section III, text-layer p.5; Table I, text-layer p.6
quotes: The results are compared against classical reinforcement learning agents, Deep Neural Networks (DNN), Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), and quantum DNN.
The quantum deep learning-based models achieved an accuracy ranging from 92.23% to 99.34%.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study that the paper reports and does not test.
assertions.reader_inference: Table I lists an IBM quantum computer as the device. The sentence does not say whether the accuracy range is for the quantum models only or what the classical models scored, so it supports no quantum advantage by itself.

assertions.value: The authors report that Rajawat et al. built the experimental setup from five IoMT devices (heart rate monitor, insulin pump, smart inhaler, pacemaker and fitness tracker), with threats such as eavesdropping, DoS and data tampering at high, medium or low vulnerability, and used quantum methods to clean the data and extract features.
quotes: They used five IoMT devices (viz., heart rate monitor, insulin pump, smart inhaler, pacemaker, and fitness tracker) to build the experimental setup
They used quantum methods to clean the data and extract features fed to the QML models
assertions.certainty_reason: A description of other work's setup.

assertions.value: The authors report that Rajawat et al. concluded that quantum computing makes it possible to rapidly process big data from IoMT devices, which QML models leverage to reduce the computation time for intricate pattern recognition significantly.
quotes: The authors concluded that quantum computing makes it possible to rapidly process big data from IoMT devices
assertions.certainty_reason: A conclusion attributed to other work.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper reports no timing measurement for this conclusion.

assertions.value: The authors report that Wang et al. proposed a Quantum Hybrid Deep Neural Network based on Deep Support Vector Data Description, trained with each class of MNIST and Fashion-MNIST in turn as normal and the rest as anomalies, and that the best AUC was 89.41% for Fashion-MNIST and 88.24% for MNIST.
assertions.anchor: Section III, text-layer p.5-6; Table I
quotes: Their idea was to train the model, considering any of the ten classes (e.g., x∈ [0, 9]) as standard and the rest as anomalies.
The best performance in terms of AUC for Fashion-MNIST was recorded as 89.41%, and MNIST was 88.24%.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study that the paper reports and does not test.
assertions.reader_inference: The text gives no AUC for the classical baseline; Table I does not list one either.

assertions.value: The authors report that Wang et al. concluded after extensive experiments that their proposed model produced better accuracy while sharing the same number of learnable parameters, and the authors repeat that a quantum model with comparable parameters can perform better than a classical network.
assertions.anchor: Section III, text-layer p.5-6; Section IV, text-layer p.7
quotes: After extensive experiments, they concluded that their proposed model produced better accuracy while sharing the same number of learnable parameters.
a quantum model with comparable parameters can perform better than a classical network [16]
assertions.certainty_reason: A conclusion attributed to one other study.
assertions.reader_inference: The survey gives neither the size of the advantage nor the baseline model.

assertions.value: The authors report that Sakhnenko et al. built a hybrid quantum-classical autoencoder with a PQC between the classical encoder and decoder, trained on 640 data points from a power plant dataset with 161 sensors, fed the compressed data to a 4-qubit PQC, and used the measured expectation values as the latent space for an isolation forest.
quotes: they chose a power plant dataset consisting of 161 sensor data monitoring the gas turbine
The HAE consists of a PQC between the classical encoder and decoder circuits.
Due to computational complexity, they train the HAE using 640 data points(1 week’s observation).
The original data is compressed by the encoder and fed into a 4-qubit PQC.
assertions.certainty_reason: A description of other work's setup.
assertions.reader_inference: The text says the training set was cut down 'due to computational complexity', which is the subsampling trend the Discussion reports.

assertions.value: The authors report that, after testing the hybrid autoencoder of Sakhnenko et al. on 2000 datapoints, the model yields 64.1% recall, and that Table I lists recall of 64.1% (gas turbine), 100% (Musk), 72.7% (Arrhythmia) and 76% (Satlog).
assertions.anchor: Section III, text-layer p.5; Table I, text-layer p.6
quotes: After testing on 2000 datapoints, the model yields 64.1% recall.
recall: 64.1% (Gas turbine) 100%(Musk) 72.7%(Arrhythmia) 76%(Satlog)
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study that the paper reports and does not test.
assertions.reader_inference: The text names the third benchmark dataset 'Satelite' and Table I names it 'Satlog'. Recall alone, with no precision or false-positive rate at that point, does not show detection quality.

assertions.value: The authors report that Sakhnenko et al. benchmarked their model on the public Musk, Arrhythmia and Satelite datasets, showing significant performance increases over a classical autoencoder in precision, recall and F1 score, and tested different PQC designs, concluding that entanglement significantly impacts model performance.
quotes: They benchmarked their model with publicly available Musk, Arrhythmia, and Satelite datasets, showing significant performance increases over classical AE in precision, recall, and F1 score.
concluding that entanglement significantly impacts model performance.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study that the paper reports and does not test.
assertions.reader_inference: The text says the study used near-term quantum computers, but Table I lists the device as a Qiskit state vector simulator. The text gives no size for 'significant'.

assertions.value: The authors report that Amin et al. (Javaria et al.) compared a quantum convolutional neural network, J-QCNN, with a classical J-DCNN on the same footing: J-DCNN accuracies were 0.97, 0.93, 0.94 and 0.90, and J-QCNN accuracies were 0.98, 0.99, 1.00 and 0.93, over four classification scenarios.
assertions.anchor: Section III, text-layer p.6; Table I
quotes: In different classification scenarios, J-DCNN showed accuracies such as 0.97 (robbery/ normal), 0.93 (abuse/ arrest/ arson/ normal), 0.94 (burglary/ explosion/ fighting/ normal), and 0.90 (stealing/shooting/shoplifting).
In contrast, J-QCNN yielded 0.98 (robbery/ normal), 0.99 (abuse/ arrest/ arson/ normal), 1.00 (burglary/ explosion/ fighting/ normal), and 0.93 (stealing/ shooting/ shoplifting).
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study that the paper reports and does not test.
assertions.reader_inference: Table I lists the device as a classical simulator. The text gives no repeat runs, confidence intervals or test-set size, so differences of 0.01 to 0.02 cannot be judged.

assertions.value: The authors state that, from the results, it is clear that QCNN outperforms the classical DCNN, and in the Discussion that in some cases quantum algorithms yield higher performance than their classical counterparts, such as J-QCNN.
assertions.anchor: Section III, text-layer p.6; Section IV key takeaways, text-layer p.7
quotes: From the results, it is clear that QCNN outperforms the classical DCNN.
In some cases, theoretically, quantum algorithms yield higher performance than their classical counterparts, such as J-QCNN [18].
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's conclusion drawn from one cited study.
assertions.reader_inference: The study ran on a classical simulator, per Table I, and the accuracy gaps are small; 'clear' is stronger than the numbers support, and 'theoretically' does not match a measured simulation.

assertions.value: The authors report that Amin et al. used the Crime-UCF dataset of video surveillance and a Crime-UNI dataset created from it, with 12,810 frames of robbery and 30,030 total frames of standard video footage, standardizing videos to the practical 10 seconds.
quotes: They chose the Crime-UCF dataset for the experiment, containing 1900 video surveillance of regular events
consisting of 12,810 frames of robbery and 30,030 total frames of standard video footage
The lengths of these videos are standardized by using only the practical 10 seconds.
assertions.certainty_reason: A description of other work's data.
assertions.reader_inference: The sentence on Crime-UNI is ambiguous about whether the 30,030 frames include the robbery frames.

assertions.value: The authors report that Kyriienko and Magnusson built a fraud detection model inspired by quantum kernels on a credit card dataset: PCA with the first N components, where N is the number of qubits, an instantaneous quantum polynomial circuit with data re-uploaded three times, a Gram matrix kernel, and a one-class support vector machine.
assertions.anchor: Section III, text-layer p.6; Table I
quotes: Initially, they use PCA and take the first N components. N is the number of qubits, which varies from a few to 20.
They have constructed the IQP circuit with data re-uploaded three times to increase the expressivity of their model.
assertions.certainty_reason: A description of other work's setup.
assertions.reader_inference: The text names the authors 'Oleksandr et al.'; reference [19] gives O. Kyriienko and E. B. Magnusson. Table I lists the device as a classical simulator on an NVIDIA A100 GPU.

assertions.value: The authors report that Kyriienko and Magnusson tested their model against unsupervised kernel-based benchmark methods and that, in the paper's words, the quantum kernel-based classifier outperforms the classical kernel in average precision, which can save millions of pounds from fraud once implemented.
assertions.anchor: Section III, text-layer p.6; Table I (best average precision, listed in the table)
quotes: The authors tested their model against unsupervised kernel-based benchmark methods
which can save millions of pounds from fraud once implemented.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result and a projected saving attributed to other work, not tested here.
assertions.reader_inference: Table I lists a best average precision of 70% for this study; the text layer holds the figure on its own line, so it is not quoted. The savings figure is a projection, with no basis given.

assertions.value: The authors report that Kyriienko and Magnusson discussed the cost of a kernel-based classifier: the Gram matrix calculation is of order Ns squared (printed flat as O(Ns2)) for Ns data points, re-evaluating the kernel for any new data takes an operation of order Ns, and inferencing Nd data costs order Nd times Ns, which increases the system's reaction time.
quotes: The main idea of any kernel-based classifier is calculating the Gram matrix, which is an O(Ns2) order operation, Ns being the number of data points.
for any new data, an operation of the order of O(Ns) will be required to re-evaluate the kernel.
for inferencing Nd number of data, the computational cost will be an order of O(NdNs)
assertions.certainty_reason: A cost analysis the paper attributes to other work and states without derivation.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer prints the square flat as 'Ns2'. The costs are those of a kernel method on a classical or quantum kernel alike; the paper does not say the quantum kernel adds to them.

assertions.value: The authors state that QML algorithms are still in their infancy and that the future emergence of fault-tolerant quantum computers will realize the industrial applications of QML algorithms in building anomaly detection systems.
assertions.anchor: Section IV key takeaways, text-layer p.7
quotes: Though QML algorithms are still in their infancy, the future emergence of fault-tolerant quantum computers will realize the industrial applications of QML algorithms in building ADS.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's forecast.
assertions.reader_inference: The sentence concedes that no industrial QML application exists yet and ties it to fault tolerance; it gives no date or evidence.

assertions.value: The authors state that mapping classical data into a complex higher dimensional quantum domain helps solve many anomaly detection problems, and that many supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning QML algorithms have been researched and found to apply to anomaly detection problems effectively.
assertions.anchor: Section IV key takeaways, text-layer p.7
quotes: Mapping classical data into a complex higher dimensional quantum domain helps solve many anomaly detection problems.
have been researched and found to apply to anomaly detection problems effectively.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's conclusion from cited studies.

assertions.value: The authors state that quantum computers are noisy and less reliable, that the error in a near-term quantum device imposes significant uncertainties during operation, that decoherence is one of the major practical problems, and that quantum error correction will be needed to envision a fault-tolerant quantum computer.
quotes: Despite quantum computers being noisy and less reliable
However, the error encountered in a near-term quantum device imposes significant uncertainties during operation.
One of the major practical problems in quantum computers is decoherence [22].
quantum error correction will be needed to envision a fault-tolerant quantum computer [23].
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement about the field and its devices, not about the paper's own work.

assertions.value: The authors state that, in the rapidly changing world, bulky classical models are inefficient in providing flexibility, whereas quantum networks are light and flexible.
quotes: bulky classical models are inefficient in providing flexibility, whereas quantum networks are light and flexible.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim; no measurement of model size or flexibility is given.
assertions.reader_inference: The Discussion says the circuits cannot handle large data volumes and the case studies subsampled their data, which sits against a claim of flexibility at scale.

assertions.value: The authors state that they expect significant research advancement in various consumer electronics domains, including anomaly detection, with the help of quantum machine learning.
quotes: we expect significant research advancement in various consumer electronics domains, including anomaly detection with the help of quantum machine learning.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's forecast.
